title: That we laugh and cry for the same thing
paragraphs: When we read in the histories that Antigonus was deeply displeased with his son for presenting him with the head of King Pyrrhus his enemy, freshly killed fighting against him, and that he wept on seeing it; that René, Duke of Lorraine, also mourned the death of Charles, Duke of Burgundy, whom he had himself defeated, and appeared in mourning at his funeral; and that at the battle of D'Auray (which Count Montfort won over Charles de Blois, his rival for the duchy of Brittany) the victor, meeting his enemy's dead body, was deeply afflicted at his death — we should not be too quick to cry:
"E cosi avven, che l'animo ciascuna Sua passion sotto 'l contrario manto, Ricopre, con la vista or'chiara, or'bruna."
["And so it happens that the soul veils each of its passions under the opposite cloak — its look now bright, now overcast." — Petrarch.]

When Pompey's head was presented to Caesar, the histories tell us, he turned his face away from it as from a sad and disagreeable sight. There had been such a long understanding and partnership between them in handling public affairs, such a community of fortunes, so many mutual services, so close an alliance, that this expression of his should not be misread, nor suspected as false or counterfeit, as this other writer would have it:
"Tutumque putavit Jam bonus esse socer; lacrymae non sponte cadentes, Effudit, gemitusque expressit pectore laeto;"
["And now he thought it safe to play the kind father-in-law — shedding forced tears and squeezing groans from a joyful breast." — Lucan, ix. 1037.]
For though it is true that most of our actions are nothing but mask and disguise, and it may sometimes be the case that
"Haeredis fletus sub persona risus est,"
["The heir's tears behind the mask are laughter." — Publius Syrus, apud Gellium, xvii. 14.]

still, in judging such episodes, we have to take into account how often our souls are stirred by several passions at once. Just as in our bodies there is, they say, a mixture of different humours, of which one is dominant according to our complexion and usually predominates in us, so the soul, though it has many motions agitating it, must necessarily have one to overrule the rest — though not with so necessary and absolute a dominion that, given the soul's pliancy and inconstancy, the less authoritative ones cannot reclaim their place on occasion and stage a little sally of their own. That is why we see not only children, who innocently follow nature, laugh and cry at the same thing, but also why none of us, on a journey we have set our heart on, can say that at the moment of parting with family and friends he doesn't feel something tugging at him inside; and even if he holds back his tears, he puts his foot in the stirrup with a sad and clouded face. And whatever gentle flame warms the heart of a modest and well-born young woman, she still has to be pried from her mother's neck and put to bed with her husband — whatever this jolly companion may say:
"Estne novis nuptis odio Venus? anne parentum Frustrantur falsis gaudia lachrymulis, Ubertim thalami quasi intra limina fundunt? Non, ita me divi, vera gemunt, juverint."

["Is Venus really so hateful to new brides, or do they cheat their parents' joy with false tears, weeping copiously almost at the very threshold of the bridal chamber? No — so help me the gods — they do not truly grieve." — Catullus, lxvi. 15.]

["Is Venus really so repugnant to newly married girls? Do they answer their parents' smiles with feigned tears? They weep copiously at the very threshold of the nuptial chamber. No — so the gods help me — they do not truly grieve." — Catullus, lxvi. 15.]

Nor is it strange to mourn someone dead whom you would by no means want alive again. When I scold my servant, I do it with all the spirit I have and load him with curses that are not pretended but downright real; yet, once the heat is over, if he should need me, I am perfectly ready to do him good — I instantly turn the page. When I call him calf and blockhead, I don't pretend to fasten those titles on him for ever; nor do I think I'm contradicting myself when, right after, I call him an honest fellow. No single quality holds us pure and entire. If it weren't a fool's habit to talk to oneself, scarcely a day or hour would go by without someone hearing me grumble and mutter to myself and against myself, "Damn fool!" — and yet I don't take that for my definition. Whoever sees me one moment cold and a moment later very affectionate toward my wife, and concludes that one or the other is faked, is an ass. Nero, taking leave of his mother whom he was sending to be drowned, was still moved at the farewell, struck with horror and pity. They say the light of the sun is not one continuous thing, but that he sends out fresh rays so densely upon one another that we cannot perceive the gaps:
"Largus enim liquidi fons luminis, aetherius sol, Irrigat assidue coelum candore recenti, Suppeditatque novo confestim lumine lumen."
["For the broad fount of liquid light, the heavenly sun, ceaselessly waters the sky with fresh brilliance, and at once supplies new light upon light." — Lucretius, v. 282.]
Just so, the soul darts out her passions variously and imperceptibly.

Artabanus, coming suddenly upon his nephew Xerxes, scolded him for the sudden change in his face. Xerxes was looking out at the immense size of his forces crossing the Hellespont for the Grecian expedition: first he was seized with a thrill of joy at seeing so many millions of men under his command, and this showed in the gaiety of his expression; but then it struck him that of all those lives, within a century at most, not one would be left — and at once his brow darkened and he grew sad, even to tears.

We have stubbornly pursued the revenge for an injury and felt a singular satisfaction at the victory; but we will still weep. We are not weeping for the victory; nothing has changed in that. But the soul looks at things with another eye and represents them to itself with another sort of face — for everything has many faces and many aspects.
Relatives, old friends, long acquaintance take hold of our imaginations and, for the time, soften them according to their condition; but the turn is so quick that it is gone in a moment:
"Nil adeo fieri celeri ratione videtur, Quam si mens fieri proponit, et inchoat ipsa, Ocius ergo animus, quam res se perciet ulla, Ante oculos quorum in promptu natura videtur;"
["Nothing seems to happen so quickly as what the mind proposes and itself begins. The mind moves faster than anything we see in nature." — Lucretius, iii. 183.]

and so, if we tried to make one continuous thing out of all this succession of passions, we would be deceiving ourselves. When Timoleon laments the murder he carried out after such mature and noble deliberation, he is not lamenting the freedom restored to his country, nor the tyrant; he is lamenting his brother. One part of his duty is done; let us allow him to do the other.
